doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Lyrics and being in the moment
title: Scatting on Four and knowing the changes
summary: Rowe praises a held note in Gates's scat; Gates calls it tedious repetition and wants to be accessible yet challenge listeners.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you were scatting last night on “Four” I took note of the one note that you held for like four bars. I think it was the last four bars of the form. You found that note, which fit every chord, and the fact that you heard that I thought was informative.

Well thank you. That comes from familiarity of the changes. If you do it over and over and over again you know what fits before you try to make it fit. You know. You know what I’m talking about. It kind of happens. If I work with students about how to do this, how do you do this, well you can call it rehearsal and you can call it practicing, but I call it tedious repetition. You do it and do it and do it and do it. It’s work. And then all of a sudden it’s not work, it’s wait a minute, I think I got it. And now it evolves into something else. Now it’s fun. So other things come to you. They just come to you if your mind is open. So you know all these changes but you know the one that’s going to work. It just does.
And you also knew that it was a good way — because it came right at the end of your choruses. And it’s like a good way to pass it on. That’s what I thought.
But you know the language though.
It sets up the next guy.

You know the language. So you hear what I’m saying, and you get it. Hopefully some people who might not know the language get it. Because I’m doing it, I mean I’m in the moment. I really am in the moment when I’m doing whatever it is that I do. And I hope they get it. But I’m not trying to exclude them. I’m trying to be accessible. But I’d like to challenge their ears at the same time. I don’t want to be like gee what just happened? I want them to go, “That was interesting, I think.”
